newsitem.title: USA: US cotton industry consensus to alter Step Two pay.
newsitem.headline: US cotton industry consensus to alter Step Two pay.

text.p: The U.S. cotton industry, after months of debate, has reached consensus to ask the government for so-called Step Two payments even if world prices are comparatively high, the National Cotton Council said on Tuesday.

The NCC board will consider the proposal on Wednesday in a closed meeting, president William Lovelady said. The meeting begins 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT). "I believe the board will agree that the adjustments are needed and will authorize the Council to pursue them in the form of technical corrections to current legislation," he said.

The centerpiece of the proposal would be elimination of a rule that bars Step Two payments whenever a special U.S. import quota, allowing more cotton to enter the country than normal, was in effect due to a 10-week run of high prices, based on USDA measurement of Northern Europe prices.

The other part of the proposal was to allow Step Two payments until the Average World Price (AWP), another USDA calculation, equals 134 percent of the loan rate. At present, payments are made until the AWP exceeds 130 percent.
The effect of the second change would be to allow Step Two payments as long as the AWP was less than 69.5 cents per lb.
"We'll look at it," Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said when asked about the proposal.
"The rationale of these changes is to make the cotton program work more in keeping with the original intent of the industry and Congress," Lovelady said in a report.

Under the 1996 farm policy law, so-called Step Two payments or certificates must be issued to users or exporters whenever the U.S.-Northern Europe price for upland cotton, calculated by USDA, is more than 1.25 cents higher than Northern Europe prices and the Average World Price does not exceed 130 percent of the loan rate.
The 1996 farm law limited Step Two expenditures to $701 million from fiscal 1996-2002.
In his report to the board, Lovelady said the ban on Step Two use whenever the special import quotas were in effect had created a "Catch 22."

"We needed certificates to make the U.S. price competitive and shut off import quotas -- which, by then, were not needed -- but we couldn't issue the certificates because the amended law prohibits issuance when an import quota opens," he said.

Producers have blamed the ban for a drop in prices last year. They say U.S. cotton was stranded at the point where it was too highly priced to compete on the world market but, because of the formula, the Step Two program could not be used.
